principles.name: Exceptional client service
principles.description: Focus on the customer, see things from their side, and build for the long term so the franchise holds up in good and bad markets.
evidence_signals: Names the customer or business user and the need behind the request
Made a decision that favored the long-term customer outcome over a quick win
Measured the result for the customer

principles.name: Operational excellence
principles.description: Set high standards, execute with skill and urgency, keep strong controls and risk discipline, and build efficient systems; act like owners.
evidence_signals: Delivered on a commitment with attention to detail and on time
Worked within controls, change management or risk rules rather than around them
Simplified a process or system and cut waste

principles.name: Integrity, fairness and responsibility
principles.description: Never compromise integrity, follow the letter and spirit of the rules, and treat people with respect and humility.
evidence_signals: Raised a concern or risk even when it was uncomfortable
Followed the rules when a shortcut was tempting, and explains why
Treats colleagues and users with respect in the story

principles.name: Face facts
principles.description: Assess reality candidly, admit mistakes, keep one version of the truth, and persist through setbacks.
evidence_signals: Admits own mistake plainly and explains what changed afterwards
Uses data to tell an unwelcome truth
Kept going after a setback and learned from it

principles.name: Great team and winning culture
principles.description: Build teamwork and loyalty, communicate honestly and clearly, put shared goals ahead of personal agendas, and lead well.
evidence_signals: Helped teammates succeed and shares credit
Communicated clearly across large or distributed teams
Gave or took honest feedback and acted on it

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Two easy-to-medium coding problems; some tracks add aptitude questions. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Recorded video interview
rounds.notes: Mainly for students and new grads: recorded behavioral prompts. Some early-career candidates then join the Code for Good hackathon, where employees observe teamwork.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: One or two medium problems in CoderPad or HackerRank plus a resume project discussion; Java questions are common. Coding part not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Superday: coding
rounds.notes: Often opens with a short code-review exercise, then a live medium problem. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Superday: system design
rounds.notes: For Associate and above. Problems tied to the bank's work, such as payments, reconciliation or rate limiting; consistency, retries, idempotency and auditability matter.

rounds.name: Superday: behavioral
rounds.notes: Production incidents, change control, working across large teams, and why this line of business.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Team fit, scope and motivation; sometimes combined with the behavioral round.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Products the candidate launched, prioritization and stakeholder management.

rounds.name: Product case
rounds.notes: A product or delivery case, such as improving a feature, measuring success or rescuing a late project.

rounds.name: Engineering partner
rounds.notes: How the candidate works with engineers, agile delivery and backlog management; not a coding round.

rounds.name: Senior leader and culture fit
rounds.notes: Several senior conversations are reported for VP-level roles.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Coding, SQL or statistics tasks. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical interview
rounds.notes: Statistics, ML fundamentals and a past project: validation, monitoring and model risk.

rounds.name: Behavioral and hiring manager
rounds.notes: Working with business partners and explaining models to non-experts.

question_patterns.pattern: A production issue the candidate caused or handled, how they communicated it and what they changed afterwards
A time a deadline pushed against a process, control or rule, and how the candidate delivered without cutting corners
Delivering something that depended on several teams or locations, and how the candidate kept everyone aligned
A change the candidate made because of a customer or business-user need, and how the result was measured
A project that was falling behind schedule and the steps the candidate took to recover it
Design a payments, reconciliation or rate-limiting service and explain how correctness is guaranteed and shown to an auditor
Explain a core Java or framework concept (collections, concurrency, garbage collection, dependency injection) and its practical effect
How the candidate would measure whether a banking feature they launched is working, and what they would do if it is not
Walk through a product or system the candidate took from idea to launch: own role, key decisions and result
Why the candidate wants this bank and this business (consumer, corporate and investment bank, asset and wealth management)

sample_questions.question: How would you design a payments backend so that a payment is never charged twice, and how would you prove it to an auditor?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify volumes, latency and failure modes. Use an idempotency key per request, a durable payment state machine (created, authorized, settled, failed) and an append-only ledger. Handle retries and timeouts with exactly-once effects, not exactly-once delivery. Add reconciliation against the payment network's records and alerts on mismatches. For audit: immutable logs, who changed what and when, and reports that tie ledger to external statements. Pitfalls: ignoring retries, or a design that mutates balances with no history.

sample_questions.question: What is the difference between a HashMap and a ConcurrentHashMap in Java, and when would you use each?
sample_questions.strong_answer: HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent writes can corrupt it or lose updates. ConcurrentHashMap allows safe concurrent reads and writes with fine-grained locking or CAS, and offers atomic operations such as computeIfAbsent and merge. It does not allow null keys or values. Use HashMap for single-threaded or confined data, ConcurrentHashMap for shared state. Mention that compound check-then-act still needs the atomic methods. Pitfalls: saying it locks the whole map, or suggesting Collections.synchronizedMap is equivalent in performance.

watch_outs: Saying it locks the whole map

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a production incident you were involved in. What happened and what did you change afterwards?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real incident and own your part. Explain detection, impact on users, how you communicated with stakeholders, how you restored service, and the root cause. Describe the lasting change: tests, monitoring, runbooks or change-control steps. In a regulated bank, show you followed process during the fix. Pitfalls: claiming you have never broken anything, blaming others, or a fix with no prevention.

sample_questions.question: Describe a time a project you were managing fell behind schedule. What steps did you take?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain why it slipped, honestly, including your part. Show how you found out early (or what you learned from finding out late), how you re-planned (scope cuts, re-sequencing, extra help), and how you told stakeholders with a realistic new date. Close with the outcome and what you now do differently. Pitfalls: heroics with no communication, or only blaming dependencies.

sample_questions.question: You launched a new feature in a banking app. How would you tell whether it is successful?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from the feature's goal and the customer problem. Define a primary metric (for example adoption or completion rate) and guardrails (complaints, fraud, call-center volume, regulatory issues). Set a baseline and a target, use an experiment or phased rollout if possible, and segment results. Say what you would do if the metric is flat: diagnose the funnel, talk to customers, iterate or roll back. Pitfalls: vanity metrics, or ignoring risk and compliance guardrails.

looking_for: Metrics tied to the feature's goal
strong_signals: A plan if results are flat
watch_outs: Vanity metrics such as page views

sample_questions.question: What is the difference between a product manager and a product owner, and how have you worked in each role?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the common distinction: the product manager owns the problem, strategy and outcomes; the product owner (often in agile teams) owns the backlog, acceptance criteria and day-to-day priorities with engineers. Note that at large banks one person may do both. Give a concrete example of each part from your work, and how you kept strategy and delivery connected. Pitfalls: textbook definitions with no personal example.

looking_for: A clear view of both roles
watch_outs: Dismissing one role as less important

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-defined tasks in an agile team with guidance; writes tested code and follows the change process.
Owns features and services within a team, designs components and handles production support.
Leads design and delivery for an application or platform area, owns production risk and mentors engineers.
Leads several teams or a platform, sets technical direction and works with senior business partners.
Owns a product area's roadmap and metrics and leads delivery with several engineering teams.

persona.tone: Professional and practical; friendly but focused on how work gets done in a large regulated bank
persona.pace: Moderate; a few questions per round with follow-ups on details
persona.pushback_style: Asks about risk, controls and production impact ('what could go wrong?', 'how would you roll it back?'); pushes for honest failures
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions about the team and line of business

case_style.notes: Only PM loops have a case. It is practical and delivery-focused: success metrics, prioritization and rescuing late projects, with risk and compliance as constraints. Engineering design rounds stress correctness and auditability.
